prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an important and timely problem: how a user can determine whether a black-box LLM API is actually serving the same distribution as a claimed reference model, or whether it has been altered through quantization, watermarking, finetuning, implementation differences, or silent updates. The paper formalizes this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem over prompt-completion pairs, proposes MMD-based tests with string kernels, and argues empirically that a simple Hamming-style kernel is particularly effective in the low-sample regime. It then applies the method to commercial APIs serving Llama-family models and reports that a substantial fraction of endpoints appear statistically distinguishable from Meta’s released weights.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and in several respects quite strong. The problem formulation is clean and useful. The empirical study is ambitious and likely to attract attention from both the ML systems and evaluation communities. The central methodological message—that for black-box LLM auditing, carefully chosen non-universal kernels can outperform more “principled” universal kernels in realistic sample regimes—is plausible and well supported by the experiments presented. The API audit case study is also compelling and likely to be impactful.

At the same time, I have several reservations that prevent me from viewing the paper as fully convincing in its current form. The main concerns are about the exact semantics of the null hypothesis in realistic API settings, the robustness of the empirical conclusions to uncontrolled confounders, the statistical calibration of the final endpoint-level decision procedure, and the extent to which the proposed Hamming kernel captures “model equality” rather than a narrower notion of surface-form similarity. I think the paper is close to being very strong, but it would benefit from sharper discussion and additional validation around these points.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem framing. “Model Equality Testing” is a useful abstraction that unifies several practical auditing questions: whether an API matches a claimed open-weight model, whether an endpoint has drifted over time, and whether two black-box systems are behaviorally equivalent on a user’s prompt distribution. This framing is simple, statistically grounded, and broad enough to be reused by others. I also appreciated that the paper explicitly focuses on sampling-based use cases rather than only greedy decoding or benchmark accuracy. That is a meaningful contribution because many real users care about the full completion distribution, not just top-1 outputs on short-answer tasks.

The methodological core is also sensible. MMD is a natural choice for black-box two-sample testing because it only requires samples and allows the practitioner to encode task-relevant similarity through the kernel. The decomposition using a prompt-matching indicator kernel is elegant and makes the test interpretable as an average discrepancy over prompts. The discussion contrasting universal kernels with coarser but more sample-efficient kernels is one of the better parts of the paper. In this setting, exact-match collisions are indeed too sparse to be useful at small N, so the empirical advantage of the Hamming kernel is believable.

The empirical evaluation in simulation is fairly extensive. The paper compares against several alternatives, varies sample size and completion length, and tests across multiple models and prompt distributions. The result that the Hamming MMD achieves useful power with roughly 10 samples per prompt is practically meaningful. The finetuning experiment is also interesting because it suggests that even modest finetuning can induce detectable shifts on unrelated prompt distributions. The model-family clustering analysis is less central, but it is a nice demonstration that the same machinery can be used for exploratory distance estimation.

The API audit section is the most attention-grabbing part of the paper, and likely the main reason many readers will care. It is valuable to see a concrete, low-cost auditing pipeline applied across many providers and models. The finding that some endpoints appear farther from the reference than entirely different model families is striking. If robust, this is an important result.

However, my main concern is that the paper sometimes overstates what can be concluded from rejection of the proposed test. The test is not checking “which model is this API serving?” in a strong identification sense; it is checking whether two induced distributions over prompt-completion pairs are equal under a particular prompt distribution, decoding setup, output representation, and kernel. This is a much narrower claim. The paper generally acknowledges dependence on prompt distribution pi, but the title, framing, and some of the discussion around provider deviations risk implying stronger attribution than the method supports. In practice, a rejection could arise from many factors besides model-weight modification: tokenizer differences, prompt templating, hidden system prompts, safety filters, stop-sequence handling, server-side truncation, nondeterministic decoding implementations, semantic caching, or even undocumented preprocessing/postprocessing. Some of these are “real” deviations from the user’s perspective, but they are not all evidence that the provider is serving a different underlying model. The paper should be much more explicit about this distinction, especially in the API audit claims.

Relatedly, the realism of the null hypothesis deserves more scrutiny. The setup assumes the auditor has sample access to a reference distribution P and an API distribution Q “with the same vocabulary and the same decoding parameters.” For commercial APIs, this assumption is fragile. Even when temperature is set to 1, providers may differ in top-p defaults, repetition penalties, stop token handling, max token semantics, chat templates, hidden system instructions, or tokenizer versions. The paper partly addresses tokenizer mismatch by moving to character space, but that only solves one piece of the problem. If the goal is to audit whether an endpoint matches released weights, then the reference implementation must match the provider’s inference stack as closely as possible, or else the test may reject for reasons orthogonal to the claimed question. The paper should provide a much more detailed accounting of how these confounders were controlled in the API experiments, and ideally ablations showing sensitivity to plausible decoding mismatches.

A second major concern is the statistical calibration of the endpoint-level audit decision. The paper first defines a level-alpha test for a single comparison, then in the API section it uses a composite null with two references (fp32 or fp16), repeats tests over ten samples, and declares failure if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. This final rule is intuitive, but it is no longer obvious what the resulting false positive rate is at the endpoint level. The paper argues that the conjunction rule over p1 and p2 controls FPR at alpha for one run, which is fine. But once the procedure is repeated ten times and thresholded by average rejection rate, the nominal significance level is no longer transparently maintained unless one assumes independence and derives the induced error probability. Moreover, Figure 1 reportedly combines prompt distributions via Bonferroni, but Table 1 uses a different reporting convention. The paper needs a clearer, end-to-end statement of the actual hypothesis test being run for each endpoint and the corresponding error control guarantee. As written, the statistical rigor of the final “11 out of 31 endpoints” claim is weaker than the earlier sections suggest.

A third concern is kernel semantics. The Hamming kernel is empirically effective, but it is also quite blunt. It measures position-wise token or character agreement and therefore emphasizes surface-form similarity. This is reasonable for detecting quantization or watermarking, but it may miss semantically meaningful distribution shifts that preserve local lexical patterns, and conversely it may flag benign stylistic or formatting differences that users may not care about. The paper acknowledges that the Hamming MMD is only a pseudometric, but the implications are underexplored. In particular, the claim that some APIs are “further from the reference than another language model” is only true under this specific pseudometric and prompt distribution. That is still interesting, but it should be framed more carefully. I would have liked to see at least one stronger semantic baseline, for example an embedding-based kernel over completions, edit-distance variants, or a hybrid kernel combining lexical and semantic similarity. Even if such baselines underperform, including them would clarify what kinds of deviations the proposed test is and is not sensitive to.

The experimental design also raises some questions. The main simulation task uses continuations of random 100-character Wikipedia snippets in multiple languages. This is a reasonable stress test for long-form generation, but it is not obvious that it reflects the distributions most relevant to API users. The paper does include HumanEval and UltraChat in the API audit, which helps, but the core kernel-selection conclusions are largely based on the Wikipedia continuation setup. It would strengthen the paper to show that the Hamming kernel remains the best choice across more diverse prompt distributions, especially instruction-following and code tasks where formatting and syntax matter differently.

I also found the comparison set somewhat incomplete. The paper compares against one-hot MMD, all-substrings MMD, and two multinomial tests. These are reasonable baselines, but they are all fairly close to the same family of exact-symbol-counting approaches. There are many other black-box two-sample tests and sequence comparison methods that could be relevant: classifier two-sample tests, energy distance on learned embeddings, n-gram feature MMD, compression-based distances, or tests based on token-level statistics if logprobs are unavailable but multiple samples per prompt are available. I do not think the paper must benchmark every possible alternative, but the current comparison may make the Hamming kernel look stronger partly because the baselines are not especially competitive for text.

Another issue is the use of simulated null p-values by repeatedly sampling from P. This is acceptable when the reference model is locally available, but one of the motivating settings is API drift over time, where old samples may be limited and resampling from the old distribution may be impossible. The paper mentions permutation tests and says trends are similar in the appendix, but this feels important enough to deserve more prominence in the main text. In many realistic auditing settings, permutation calibration is the only viable option. If it materially reduces power, that tradeoff should be front and center.

The paper’s claims about effect size and correlation with task accuracy are interesting but should be interpreted cautiously. The moderate correlation between Hamming MMD and HumanEval accuracy difference is not surprising, but it is also not especially strong. More importantly, MMD is not directly a utility metric; a large MMD can reflect many stylistic differences with little downstream impact, while a small MMD can hide rare but catastrophic failures. The paper does mention this, but some of the narrative around “serious deviations” could be more nuanced. I would encourage the authors to separate clearly the roles of the method as a hypothesis test, as a descriptive distance, and as a proxy for task degradation.

There are also some presentation and clarity issues. The paper is generally well written, but a few parts could be sharpened. The distinction between token-space and character-space testing appears in different sections and could be consolidated. The exact normalization of the Hamming kernel and whether it is unit-norm, as assumed earlier for MMD exposition, should be clarified. The computational complexity of the different kernels and the practical runtime of the audit pipeline should be stated more explicitly in the main text. The paper would also benefit from a concise discussion of what an auditor should do after rejection: how to diagnose the source of deviation, how many prompts to use, and how to choose a kernel for a specific application.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has substantial merit. The problem is important, the framing is useful, and the empirical findings are provocative. My overall assessment is positive but not unreservedly so. The work is strongest as a practical auditing framework for detecting distributional non-equivalence under user-chosen prompts and representations. It is weaker if interpreted as identifying the underlying model or attributing deviations specifically to provider-side model modifications.

To strengthen the paper, I would most strongly recommend the following. First, tighten the claims throughout to emphasize that the method tests equality of induced output distributions under a specified audit protocol, not identity of underlying weights or architectures. Second, provide a more rigorous account of the endpoint-level statistical procedure, including the actual false positive guarantee after repetition and aggregation. Third, add more detail and, if possible, ablations on API confounders such as top-p, stop sequences, hidden prompts, and formatting differences. Fourth, include at least one semantic or embedding-based baseline kernel to better characterize the sensitivity profile of the Hamming approach. Fifth, elevate the permutation-based calibration results into the main paper if that is the realistic deployment setting for many users.

In summary, this is a strong and timely paper with a compelling application and a sensible methodological core. Its main contribution is not a fundamentally new statistical test, but rather a useful formalization of LLM API auditing plus a convincing empirical case that simple MMD tests with appropriate string kernels can work surprisingly well in practice. The main weaknesses are overinterpretation of what rejection means, incomplete treatment of real-world confounders, and some looseness in the final statistical reporting. If these issues are addressed, I think the paper could become a valuable reference for black-box model auditing.

My recommendation would be a weak accept to borderline accept, depending on the conference bar and on whether the authors can clarify the statistical guarantees and temper the causal interpretation of the API audit results.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper formalizes auditing black-box LLM APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem called Model Equality Testing. Given samples from a reference model distribution and an API distribution under matched prompts and decoding settings, the goal is to test whether the conditional completion distributions are equal. The authors propose using MMD-based kernel two-sample tests, with a simple Hamming-style string kernel over completions as the main practical choice. Through simulations on quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model substitution, they show this test has substantially better small-sample power than one-hot, substring, and multinomial baselines, reporting median 77.4% power with roughly 10 samples per prompt. They then audit 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama models and report that 11 endpoints appear statistically different from Meta reference weights (allowing either fp32 or fp16 as nulls). The paper also uses estimated MMD values as effect-size proxies to compare model families and provider deviations.
strengths: Timely and practically important problem: black-box API auditing for LLMs is highly relevant for reproducibility, benchmarking, and user trust.
Clear problem formulation as a conditional two-sample testing task, which unifies several auditing scenarios such as provider substitution and temporal drift.
Method is simple, computationally feasible, and does not require log-probability access, making it broadly deployable.
Empirical study is extensive in scope: multiple distortions, multiple open and closed models, multiple prompt distributions, and a real-world audit of commercial providers.
The Hamming-kernel MMD baseline is intuitive and appears empirically strong in the low-sample regime compared with exact-match and multinomial alternatives.
The paper goes beyond binary testing by estimating pairwise distances/effect sizes between models and APIs, which is useful for interpretation.
Open-sourcing code and a large completion dataset increases reproducibility and potential impact.
weaknesses: The main methodological contribution is relatively modest: the core test is standard MMD with a hand-designed kernel, and much of the novelty lies in the application domain.
The chosen Hamming kernel is not characteristic/universal, so the test is not consistent against all alternatives; this limitation is acknowledged but weakens the generality of the claims.
The empirical prompt distributions used for core simulations are somewhat artificial (random Wikipedia continuations) and may not reflect many realistic API use cases.
The API audit conclusions may be confounded by imperfect control of decoding details, tokenizer differences, system-side prompt formatting, stop conditions, or undocumented sampling implementations.
The decision rule for endpoint failure (average rejection rate over 10 repeated tests >= 0.5) is heuristic and not tied to a clearly analyzed statistical guarantee.

The paper emphasizes power but gives limited finite-sample calibration evidence for Type I error under the exact practical pipeline, especially in character-space testing and repeated-test aggregation.

Interpretation of detected differences is sometimes stronger than warranted: rejecting equality does not identify the cause (quantization, watermarking, routing, prompt preprocessing, safety layers, etc.).
methodological_flaws: Equation (4) appears to mix an unbiased within-sample U-statistic term with a cross-sample term normalized by N^2; this is standard for equal sample sizes, but the notation 'sum over z,z' in D_P' should explicitly exclude diagonal terms to avoid ambiguity. As written, the estimator definition is slightly imprecise.

The composite-null testing rule in Section 5 controls FPR by rejecting only when both p-values are below alpha, but the proof sketch is informal and does not address dependence between p1 and p2. The conclusion still holds via P(A∩B) <= P(A), but the written argument using conditional probability is unnecessarily loose and could mislead.

The endpoint-level aggregation rule ('repeat tests over ten samples and fail if average rejection rate >= 0.5') lacks a formal hypothesis-testing justification. This can distort the nominal significance level and makes the reported 11/31 failures harder to interpret statistically.

Character-space comparison across APIs is practical, but it changes the estimand relative to token-space model equality. Two APIs could be token-distribution equivalent yet differ after decoding normalization, or vice versa; this mismatch is not fully analyzed.

Power comparisons may be sensitive to kernel scaling and implementation details. The paper compares several tests, but it is unclear whether all baselines were equally tuned for this domain, which may bias conclusions in favor of the proposed kernel.

The empirical validity of the real-world audit depends critically on exact matching of decoding parameters and prompt formatting across providers and local reference inference. Since many APIs implement temperature, truncation, stop tokens, and chat templates differently, some detected differences may reflect interface mismatch rather than model modification.

Using random Wikipedia prefixes as the main simulation benchmark may overstate generality. The claim that the method broadly audits user tasks is only partially validated, since realistic distributions with structured prompts, long-context chat formatting, or tool-use behavior are not systematically studied.
